source.title_on_document: Evaluating TRIZ with and without LLM support: an experimental study on engineering problem-solving

supplement.holds: The paper refers to no supplement or online appendix (the text layer of all 10 pages has no 'supplement' or 'appendix'). All design-quality statistics are in the main text (Section 4.2 and Table 2, p. 512). Data and materials are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request (Data availability, p. 515).

paper_design_summary: Engineering students each solved one of three engineering concept problems (polymer gear testing rig GT, bicycle drive mounting bracket MB, wind turbine power maximization WT) and were randomly assigned to use the TRIZ contradiction matrix with an LLM assistant (TRIZ-C+LLM: Microsoft Copilot with Smart GPT-5 recommended, plus a prompt pack) or the TRIZ contradiction matrix alone (TRIZ-C: the triz40.com site, no LLM); 114 students were analyzed. Experts holding PhDs in mechanical engineering rated each student's final developed solution on feasibility, requirements, innovativeness, and elaboration (1-7), averaged into a design-quality score. A post-task survey measured self-reported workload, usefulness, and satisfaction.

studies.label: TRIZ-C+LLM vs TRIZ-C experiment on three engineering problems (GT, MB, WT)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Method: the TRIZ contradiction matrix with an LLM-based AI assistant (TRIZ-C+LLM) or the TRIZ contradiction matrix only (TRIZ-C), assigned at random to each student, who solved one problem only. The problem was not randomized: each problem was solved by a different student group (Group 2 GT and Group 3 MB at Location 2, Group 4 WT at Location 3; GT and MB were part of a course). The randomization procedure is not described.
assignment.quote: Each student solved one problem only and was randomly assigned the method to use, either TRIZ-C+LLM or TRIZ-C.
assignment.locator: p. 510 (PDF p. 4), Section 3.2.1; groups and locations in Figure 2

arms.name: TRIZ-C+LLM
arms.description: TRIZ contradiction matrix supported by an LLM-based AI assistant. Students received a prompt pack (problem framing, contradiction parameters, inventive principles, solution generation, diversity check) and were recommended Microsoft Copilot with Smart GPT-5, but were free to choose another assistant if they reported it. Analyzed per problem: GT 10, MB 10, WT 43 (Table 2).

arms.name: TRIZ-C
arms.description: TRIZ contradiction matrix only, with access to https://www.triz40.com/ and instructions not to use any LLM-based AI assistant. Analyzed per problem: GT 11, MB 10, WT 30 (Table 2).

participants.exclusions: One GT student did not understand the engineering problem and was excluded from the study (Table 1 note). Table 1 lists 22 GT students by curriculum (ME 22) and by year of study (20 + 2) against N1 = 21; the paper does not say whether this student had been assigned a method, or to which arm. The paper gives no count at assignment. Design quality is analyzed for 114 (51 TRIZ-C, 63 TRIZ-C+LLM; Table 2). One MB TRIZ-C+LLM student did not answer the survey, so survey analyses use 113 (62 vs 51; Table 2 and p. 513). A pilot (Group 1, Location 1) tested the protocol; it reports no sample size and is not analyzed.
participants.who: Engineering students. GT: mainly fourth-year mechanical engineering students (Table 1: ME 22; year 4 = 20, year 5 = 2; N1 = 21 after the exclusion). MB: Erasmus exchange master students, most with a mechanical engineering background (Table 1: ME 12, IE 4, GE 3; the curriculum and year-of-study counts each sum to 19; N1 = 20, N2 = 19). WT: fourth- and fifth-year industrial engineering students specialized in AI, with a common mechanical engineering background (73).
participants.country: not_stated (Figure 2 names Location 2 for GT and MB, Location 3 for WT, and Location 1 for the pilot, without naming countries; author affiliations: Slovenia, Sweden, Morocco, Canada)
participants.quote: N1: number of students performing the assignment, N2: number of students answering the questionnaire ... *One student did not understand the engineering problem and was therefore excluded from the study.
participants.locator: p. 510 (PDF p. 4), Table 1 and note; p. 512 (PDF p. 6), Table 2

ai_tool.name_model: Microsoft Copilot with the LLM option Smart GPT-5 (recommended); students were free to choose other LLM-based AI assistants but had to report which one. The paper does not report which assistants were used.
ai_tool.how_used: Students prompted the chatbot with a prompt pack of instructions and examples for problem framing, identifying TRIZ contradiction parameters, suggesting inventive principles, generating solutions, and a diversity check, then developed and documented their most promising idea (p. 511, Section 3.3, Figure 3). Before the task all participants had a 30 min TRIZ presentation, a 15 min prompt-engineering presentation, and a practice problem.

task.description: Engineering concept problems solved individually with the TRIZ contradiction matrix: GT, a concept for alternating loading of polymer gears in a test rig; MB, a bracket for mounting a specified electrical drive onto a bicycle frame; WT, a concept to maximize wind turbine power (the power equation was given). Students searched for and selected contradictions. In WT a contradiction and its principles were then imposed and ideas were based on at least three inventive principles; in GT and MB students worked with contradictions and principles of their choice. Students then developed and documented their top-ranked idea.
task.duration: Test planned to take about 45 minutes (students could use more or less time), preceded by a 30 min TRIZ presentation, 15 min of prompt engineering, and a practice problem (p. 511, Section 3.3). Reported completion time: TRIZ-C+LLM M = 40.3 min (SD 20.9), TRIZ-C M = 46.2 min (SD 21.3) (p. 513).

outcomes.name: Design quality (expert-rated; mean of feasibility, requirements, innovativeness, elaboration)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Experts holding PhDs in mechanical engineering rated each student's final solution on four criteria on a 1-7 scale: C1 feasibility, C2 requirements (how well the solution meets technical criteria and requirements), C3 innovativeness of solution, C4 elaboration; design quality is the average of the four. GT and MB: two experts with prior experience in the problem domains, not personally involved in the problem, rated independently and their scores were averaged per criterion; WT: another independent expert rated all solutions. Only the composite is reported, not the separate criteria, and blinding to condition is not stated. Coded usefulness because the paper calls the score design quality and the codebook lists quality and feasibility under usefulness; innovativeness (novelty) and elaboration are two of the four criteria. Analysis: two-way ANOVA (Problem x Method) with simple effects. The Total rows of Table 2 pool the problems in different proportions across arms (WT is 43 of 63 TRIZ-C+LLM students and 30 of 51 TRIZ-C students), so they are not the means that the Method main-effect test compares (first contrast). No inter-rater agreement is reported.

contrasts.treatment_arm: TRIZ-C+LLM (all three problems, Method main effect of the two-way ANOVA)
contrasts.control_arm: TRIZ-C (all three problems, Method main effect of the two-way ANOVA)
contrasts.reported: Two-way ANOVA (Problem x Method), Method main effect: F(1, 108) = 3.21, p = .076, 'which is not significant'. Problem x Method interaction F(2, 108) = 7.58, p = .001. Problem main effect F(2, 108) = 27.89, p < .001. Levene's test F(5, 108) = 2.88, p = .018. The paper prints no arm means for this test. The Total rows of Table 2 (TRIZ-C 4.8, SD 0.90, N 51 vs TRIZ-C+LLM 5.6, SD 1.13, N 63) weight each problem by its cell size, and WT, the highest-scoring problem, is 30 of 51 TRIZ-C and 43 of 63 TRIZ-C+LLM students. The paper does not test the gap between the Total rows. A back-calculation from Table 2 (not printed) matches F = 3.21 to the unweighted mean of the three per-problem gaps, about 0.3 points (the rounded cell means give 4.7 vs 5.0), and not to the 0.8-point gap between the Total rows, which would give F of about 27.5. Do not pair the Total rows with this test or compute an effect size from them. Contrasts 2 to 4 carry the arm means, SDs, and Ns.
contrasts.locator: p. 512 (PDF p. 6), Section 4.2 and Table 2 (Total block and the six problem-by-method cells)

contrasts.reported: GT: TRIZ-C 4.9 (SD 0.91, N 11) vs TRIZ-C+LLM 4.6 (SD 1.17, N 10); simple effect F(1, 108) = .51, p = .479.
MB: TRIZ-C 4.2 (SD 0.98, N 10) vs TRIZ-C+LLM 4.2 (SD 0.93, N 10); simple effect F(1, 108) = .06, p = .809.
WT: TRIZ-C 5.0 (SD 0.78, N 30) vs TRIZ-C+LLM 6.2 (SD 0.62, N 43); simple effect F(1, 108) = 34.67, p < .001.

company_involvement.description: No company involvement stated. The LLM arm was recommended Microsoft Copilot, but the paper describes no role for Microsoft. data_and_code.data_url: Available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request (p. 515, Data availability)

eligibility.reason: Students were randomly assigned individually to TRIZ with an LLM assistant or TRIZ alone (p. 510, Section 3.2.1); 114 students were analyzed for design quality, 51 TRIZ-C and 63 TRIZ-C+LLM (Table 2, p. 512); experts rated each student's solution, produced with the LLM available in the treatment arm, on four criteria that include innovativeness. Caveats: the randomization procedure is not described and the WT arms are uneven (43 vs 30); the problem was not randomized, and each problem was solved by a different student group (GT and MB at Location 2, WT at Location 3); only WT (73) exceeds 50 on its own, with GT 21 and MB 20; the outcome is a composite quality score, not a creativity rating alone.

one_line_finding: In a two-way ANOVA of expert-rated design quality (1-7), the LLM's main effect across the three problems was not significant (F(1, 108) = 3.21, p = .076), and method interacted with problem (F(2, 108) = 7.58, p = .001): the LLM raised quality on the general WT problem (6.2 vs 5.0, F(1, 108) = 34.67, p < .001) but not on the specialized GT (4.6 vs 4.9, p = .479) or MB (4.2 vs 4.2, p = .809) problems (p. 512, Section 4.2 and Table 2).
open_questions: Construct coding: design quality averages feasibility, requirements, innovativeness, and elaboration. Coded usefulness (the paper calls it design quality, and the codebook lists quality and feasibility under usefulness, as in the c003 reconciliation); overall_creativity or other are defensible. Innovativeness (C3) alone is not reported.
Design class: coded lab_rct (one test protocol run at each site after presentations and a practice problem); GT and MB were part of a course, which could argue for field_rct for those 41 students.

Randomization: the paper states random assignment but gives no procedure; the WT arms are 43 vs 30, uneven for simple 1:1 assignment. Under 1:1 assignment, a split at least this uneven has a two-sided probability of about 0.16 (the checkers' arithmetic, not printed), so it does not contradict the stated randomization.

Whether the problem groups should be separate samples or studies: each problem was solved by a different student group (GT and MB at Location 2, WT at Location 3), the paper analyzes them jointly in one two-way ANOVA, and only WT (73) passes the 50-person rule alone. If S1 stays one sample, Review 1 also chooses which record it contributes: the pooled Method main effect, which has only a test statistic (the Total rows of Table 2 do not match it), or the per-problem contrasts, which have arm means, SDs, and Ns.

Count at assignment: Table 1 lists 22 GT students by curriculum and year but N1 = 21 after one exclusion; the paper does not say whether the excluded student had been assigned a method, or to which arm.

Confounding named by the authors: the WT students specialized in AI and were more experienced in prompting, so the WT effect may reflect problem difficulty, prompting experience, or both (pp. 510, 514).
notes: Self-reported outcomes are not listed because they are not scored on the output (form B listed satisfaction with results as S1-O2). Satisfaction with the final result (Table 2, in parentheses): Total TRIZ-C 4.3 (SD 1.44, N 51) vs TRIZ-C+LLM 4.7 (SD 1.22, N 62); GT 4.4 (1.75) vs 3.7 (1.25); MB 3.7 (1.25) vs 4.0 (0.87, N 9); WT 4.5 (1.36) vs 5.1 (1.07); t-test p = .119; correlation with the expert scores ρ(113) = 0.38, p < .001 (p. 513). Workload: difficulty defining contradictions TRIZ-C+LLM M = 3.18 (SD 1.52) vs TRIZ-C M = 4.37 (SD 1.55), t(111) = −4.123, p < .001, d = −0.779; overall problem difficulty 3.31 (SD 1.36) vs 4.27 (SD 1.34), t(111) = −3.784, p < .001, d = −0.715; mental effort (MB and WT students only) problem-by-method interaction F(1,88) = 6.89, p = .048 (as printed: F(1, 88) = 6.89 gives p of about .010, so the printed F or p is wrong). No significant differences for perceived usefulness (p = .133), use TRIZ again (p = .541), time sufficiency (p = .307), clarity of instructions (p = .766), innovation gain (p = .321), quality of the generated ideas (p = .099), feasibility perception (p = .945), or enjoyment (p = .271); Figure 4 shows means with SE bars (p. 513). The pilot (Group 1, Location 1) tested the protocol on GT and WT with Microsoft Copilot GPT-5 and reports no sample size or outcome data. Students in the LLM arm could use assistants other than Copilot; the paper does not report which were used. Table 2 prints means to one decimal and SDs to two decimals. Comparison type ai_vs_bau: both arms used the TRIZ contradiction matrix, and the control had the triz40.com site and no LLM.

differences.resolved: usefulness (B). The paper names the score design quality and never calls it creativity, and the codebook lists quality and feasibility under usefulness. Two of the four averaged criteria (feasibility, requirements) are usefulness criteria; innovativeness (novelty) and elaboration are the other two, which measure_detail and open_questions record. The c003 reconciliation coded an overall-quality judgment that included novelty the same way.

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-O1 contrast 1 paired the Total rows of Table 2 (TRIZ-C 4.8 vs TRIZ-C+LLM 5.6, which weight the problems by unequal cell sizes) with the ANOVA Method main-effect test (F(1, 108) = 3.21, p = .076) and direction no_clear_difference, but that test compares unweighted problem-cell means, a gap of about 0.3 points. one_line_finding repeated the pairing.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: Confirmed against Table 2 and Section 4.2 (p. 512). The Total rows are the cell-size-weighted means of the problem cells (4.82 and 5.63). With the within-cell error variance from the Table 2 SDs (0.656 on 108 df), the printed simple-effect F values imply per-problem gaps of -0.25 (GT), +0.09 (MB, the sign that reproduces the main effect), and +1.13 (WT). Their unweighted mean, 0.32, gives F = 3.21. A cell-size-weighted adjusted gap (0.69) would give F of about 20, and the 0.8-point Total gap would give F of about 27.5. Contrast 1 is now labeled as the Method main effect of the two-way ANOVA, and its statistics_available is test_statistic only (it was arm_means_sds_ns and test_statistic). Its reported field keeps every printed number and says that the paper prints no arm means for this test, that the paper does not test the Total rows, and that they are not to be used for an effect size. Direction stays no_clear_difference, which follows the paper's test. measure_detail now points to contrast 1, one_line_finding no longer pairs 5.6 vs 4.8 with p = .076, and open question 4 notes which record S1 contributes. Contrasts 2 to 4 are unchanged.
challenge_resolution.quote: Regarding the main effect of the Method factor, the following values were obtained: F(1, 108) = 3.21, p = .076, which is not significant.
challenge_resolution.locator: p. 512 (PDF p. 6), Section 4.2 and Table 2 (Total block and the six problem-by-method cells)

open_items.item: Construct of the design-quality composite (open question 1): coded usefulness, with overall_creativity or other defensible. Innovativeness (C3) is not reported alone. Under any of these codes, experts scored each student's output, so criterion 3 holds either way. A separate novelty record would need the per-criterion scores, which the paper offers only on request from the corresponding author.
Design class (open question 2): coded lab_rct. GT and MB (41 students) were part of a course, which could argue for field_rct for them. Both are core design classes.

Randomization (open question 3): random assignment of each student is stated, but no procedure is given. The WT arms are 43 vs 30, a split with a two-sided probability of about 0.16 under 1:1 assignment (checkers' arithmetic). Criterion 1 rests on the stated random assignment.

Problem groups as samples (open question 4): each problem was solved by a separate student group, and the paper analyzes them jointly in one two-way ANOVA. Treated as separate samples, GT (21 analyzed) and MB (20) fall below 50, but WT (73) still meets all three criteria, so core holds either way. Review 1 decides the sample ids and which record S1 contributes.

Count at assignment (open question 5): one GT student was excluded for not understanding the problem, and the paper does not say whether this student had been assigned a method, or to which arm, so n_randomized stays null. Criterion 2 counts the 114 analyzed either way.

Problem confounded with student group (open question 6): the WT students specialized in AI and were more experienced in prompting, so the WT effect may reflect problem difficulty, prompting experience, or both (pp. 510, 514). Method was randomized within each group, so each per-problem contrast is still a randomized comparison. This study cannot separate the two explanations.
